Equation (6.1.1) is an example of a ‘differential equation’. It cannot be simply integrated as the right-hand side involves the unknown function A(t) . The reaction rate is kA , i.e. it is proportional to the amount of A. The reaction also uses up the species A and so the reaction rate determines the rate at which A is lost. Therefore, the rate of change of species A,  rac{{m d}A}{{m d}t} , is equal to the negative of the reaction rate, -kA . Now, consider a simple bimolecular reaction between gases A+B	o	ext{products} where A(t) and B(t) are the concentrations of A and B respectively. The reaction rate depends on the concentrations of A and B and so the concentration of species A (assuming fixed volume) changes as  rac{{m d}A}{{m d}t}=-{k}_{AB}AB\,. If the reaction starts with concentrations A={A}_{0} and B={B}_{0} , then at time t , the same number of A and B molecules will be used up, so {A}_{0}-A={B}_{0}-B , and hence B={B}_{0}+A-{A}_{0} . Therefore, the reaction rate is now a quadratic function of A  rac{{m d}A}{{m d}t}=-{k}_{AB}A({B}_{0}+A-{A}_{0}) It is possible the reaction rate may be even more complicated. It may also depend on temperature, which may depend simply on time or even on the reaction itself, e.g.  rac{{m d}A}{{m d}t}=-{k}_{AB}(t)A({B}_{0}+A-{A}_{0}) Ordinary differential equations (ODEs) An ordinary differential equation (ODE) is an equation linking a variable (say t ), a function (say y ) and its derivatives  rac{{m d}y}{{m d}t} ,  rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}t^{2}} , etc. f\left(t,y, rac{{m d}y}{{m d}t}, rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}t^{2}},\ldots% ight)=0 The term “ordinary” distinguishes this from other types of differential equation, such as partial differential equations (where the functions depend on more than one variable). We will only consider ODEs in this course. Order of Differential Equations. The highest derivative present determines the order of the differential equation. •​A first-order equation is of the form f_{1}\left(t,y, rac{{m d}y}{{m d}t}ight)=0\,, for example,  rac{{m d}A}{{m d}t}=-kA . •​A second-order equation is of the form f_{2}\left(t,y, rac{{m d}y}{{m d}t}, rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}t^{2}}% ight)=0\,, for example,  rac{{m d}^{2}A}{{m d}t^{2}}=-m^{2}A . We will focus on first and second order ODEs in this course. Example 6.1.1 (Lecture). Find the order of the following ODEs. (a)​ \displaystyle rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=1+x^{2}y^{2} (b)​ \displaystyle rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}t^{2}}=-ky (c)​ \displaystyle\left( rac{{m d}^{3}z}{{m d}t^{3}}ight)^{7}+\left( rac{{% m d}^{5}z}{{m d}t^{5}}ight)^{4}=z^{12} Solution (a)​1st order (b)​2nd order (c)​5th order Solutions to differential equations. To ‘solve’ a differential equation, e.g. {f}_{1}\left(t,y, rac{{m d}y}{{m d}t}ight)=0 we need to write it in a form without the derivative (preferably in explicit form), e.g. g\left(y,tight)=0 or preferably y=h(t) . Consider the differential equation  rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=xy It can be seen that y=\exp({x}^{2}/2) is a solution. Using the chain rule gives equation equation However, we also see that \displaystyle y=5\exp({x}^{2}/2) is a solution, since \displaystyle rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=5x{e}^{ rac{{x}^{2}}{2}} and \displaystyle xy=5x{e}^{ rac{{x}^{2}}{2}} . Also, y=0 is a solution, since in this case \displaystyle rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=0 and xy=0 . In fact, anything in the form y=C{e}^{ rac{{x}^{2}}{2}} where C is an arbitrary constant, is a solution to \displaystyle rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=xy . This is called the general solution of this differential equation. General and particular solutions A first-order differential equation will have a solution involving an arbitrary constant. This is called the general solution. If the value of the constant is known, the solution is called a particular solution. The particular solution can be found if one additional piece of information exists. For first order ODEs this extra piece of information is usually known as the initial condition. A second-order ODE is an equation of the form f\left(x,y, rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}, rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}x^{2}}ight)=0 An example application is modelling mechanical oscillations, such as those shown in Figure 6.2. Linear 2nd order ODE with constant coefficients We will consider 2nd order ODEs that can be written in the form a rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}x^{2}}+b rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}+cy=f(x) where a , b , and c are constants. Homogeneous case Take the special case when the right-hand side is zero a rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}x^{2}}+b rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}+cy=0 This is known as the homogeneous case. This should not be confused with homogeneous first-order ODEs in Section 6.4. For particular values of m y={e}^{mx} is a solution of this ODE. If y={e}^{mx} , then  rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}=m{e}^{mx} and  rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}x^{2}}={m}^{2}{e}^{mx} . The equation a rac{{m d}^{2}y}{{m d}x^{2}}+b rac{{m d}y}{{m d}x}+cy=0 becomes {e}^{mx}\left(a{m}^{2}+bm+cight)=0 This is only satisfied if m is a solution to the quadratic a{m}^{2}+bm+c=0\,. Therefore, {y}_{1}={e}^{{m}_{1}x} and {y}_{2}={e}^{{m}_{2}x} are both solutions of the ODE. If the roots are real and distinct ( {m}_{1}
